comments.author: cochne
comments.text:
This is an amazing and unexpected result.  To be clear though, it does not imply that NP is subexponential: "Note that runtime bounds of the form 2^o(n) do not transfer under general polynomial-time reductions (2^n^o(1) would be needed for this), so our result does not imply that general NP problems
admit subexponential time algorithms."
Edit: To explain more, it is guaranteed that you can
reduce
any NP problem to 3SAT in polynomial time with a polynomial factor in input size.  You still have to solve it.
If 3SAT were solvable in polynomial time, then polynomial(polynomial(x)) = polynomial(x) and you're implied to have an overall polynomial time solution.
But what we have here is that 3SAT is solveable in subexponential time.  subexponential(polynomial(x)) is not guaranteed to be sub-exponential.
Further edit: The subexponential solution
does
carry over to any (?) problems that have can be reduced to 3SAT in a linear number of variables.  They list: Counting independent sets, Counting proper q-colorings, Counting perfect matchings.

This construction splits the space into 'small' models with a quadratic lookup cost and 'large' with sub-exponential cost. The small one is by enumerating all SAT problems with their answers, then looking up the answer. The large one is something in polynomials I don't understand. An answer from openai about where the cutoff is was:
the constructed lookup machine has vastly more states than the estimated total number of physically distinguishable configurations of the observable universe.

comments.author: mattbee
comments.text:
I just resurrected a 90s kids CD-ROM game that shipped for Windows 3.1 -
https://github.com/matthewbloch/orlys-draw-a-story-fixes
The finished patch DLL ended up being a tour of the stuff that broke.
The game did launch on Windows 11 but the main issue was that the 8-bit pre-DirectDraw behaviour was broken - for 256 colour screens, Windows 11 resolvesld palette indices only once, but the game relies on being able to change the palette for fades etc. Most of the screeen ended up black, but you could see the animated parts just fine.
So most of fix ended up being to hook every draw call and implement a virtual GDI that acted like a graphics card of the day.
There was a 32-bit disc space check that overflowed, a couple of use-after-free crashes and some racey threading calls that can't have been tested on a machine with 2 CPUs.
Backwards compatibility from Microsoft was almost all there, and probably would have kept Orly running for a couple of subsequent Windows releases. But it relies on a developer meeting them half-way, it's not an emulation layer.

Everything comes back to whether the demand is really there.
Anthropic thinks it is. The got the demand / datacenter match right in Q2, got great margins, and committed hard.

There are three issues with this. First, the rapid diffusion of the technology means it is very unlikely to continue at the rate of adoption seen over the past year, so it's very hard to extrapolate based on what we've seen so far. Second, many companies are reigning in AI budgets after an initial honeymoon phase. Third, all of the other labs are trying to take a bite of the coding pie, and the price war is already heating up.

Getting out and exploring the natural world is great and I highly recommend it, but even for people without the opportunity or inclination to get out there birding is still extremely accessible.
Everyone can see birds around their home or work. Getting started can be as simple as noticing which birds you see regularly and figuring out what kind they are, and how the males and females differ in appearance (or don't). Usually males are the prettier more colorful ones, which is an effective signal for fitness.
Common birds will be easy to identify. Figuring out unusual birds or behaviors can turn into quite the detective project.
From there you can start to recognize calls and behavioral patterns. Once you learn a little bit in those areas it can be like seeing in another dimension. It's neat to hear a particular call and immediately know that there is a hawk in a nearby tree, or a cat behind a car.

comments.author: cmrx64

Once I started paying attention and interacting with more birds I got hooked.
It really is a very different cognitive mode. And when LLMs later came out I took my birdwatching-stance into it, which felt like a natural way to encounter some new entities.
I find it easy to believe that birdwatching is fairly distinctive in how it organizes the brain. Many sibling comments were wondering “is it the bird watching or is it an isolatable factor.” Bird watching is an extremely distinctive sensory integration, prediction, classification, etc task with lots of subproblems yes but also binding them in an irreducible way with agency detection (a vital part of cognition that modern environments are impoverished of) and attention.

comments.author: mkakkori

Working with Claude didn't atrophy his spotting skills, it was more like having a good experienced partner. When I went on a birding trip with him and a goshawk flew by, he already knew what Claude had told him earlier about the identifying marks, and that's what he tried to capture better this time.

stories.title_en: Fixing Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.text:
Constrained decoding has been in vLLM for a long time, and constrained tool call decoding has been in vLLM for a while, too.
The blog post is rather confusing because until you understand the entire situation it appears to imply that they fixed vLLM (what the title implies) but really they just needed to configure it correctly.
To be fair, the course of constrained tool calling configuration in vLLM changed over time in ways that changed behavior, which is the real problem. The Ubicloud team deserves a lot of credit for having benchmarks in place to track performance and catch regressions for investigations. Some of the providers you find on OpenRouter have inexplicably bad performance relative to others and clearly do not care this much.
However, if this article left you confused because constrained decoding and constrained tool call schema have been features in vLLM for a long time, jump to the end where they show what configuration changes they made.

comments.author: mmastrac
comments.text:
Amusingly constrained decoding is the same approach we use to turn an AR model into a /v1/systemone endpoint (I worked on the vLLM feature).
Tool calling is fraught with peril, especially because there's nothing that necessarily says that a models tools are fixed in place for the life of its run.
In some cases, tools are added mid-run to avoid a giant prefix miss and (at least last time I checked!), the industry has not settled on OpenAI-style chat message formats for tool call updates.
I would absolutely prefer to run in a fully-constrained tool call environment, and would love if we hadn't YOLO'd the whole thing! The PTC-style tools sort of fix this by punting tool calling to JavaScript, but that's even harder to enforce, and models not trained on the style might take a turn of failed tool calls to get it right.

comments.author: hansvm
comments.text: I wish they'd published something about the actual impact on model quality. Schema-constrained decoding changes the distribution the LLM will output. I'd be curious how a back-up-and-retry method for tool calls (which also doesn't pollute the context and also has 100% tool-call accuracy) would compare. In their example stats (23/25 success rate), it'd be +9% tokens used for the tool call attempt itself, but that's +9% on just a small fraction of the total tokens, so if a retry solution gave any better accuracy I think it might win out.

comments.author: jesdo
comments.text: I'm one of the authors of this blog post. Figuring out how to integrate the LLM, the inference and serving engine, and the constrained decoding implementation such that you get the intended output and overall quality definitely requires careful engineering and testing. Please feel free to AMA. :)

comments.author: docjay
comments.text:
That is bending the barrel to align the scope. What’s interesting is that the authors mention the cause of the failed calls, “…a model may generate a tool or field name that it has seen during the training, even if it does not exist in the current production environment. For example, it may generate search_web when the available tool is web_search, or use city_name when the active schema expects location”, but then failed to see that it’s also the solution. If you call it “web_search” but it calls it as “search_web” then just rename your function to “search_web” and let the problem resolve itself.
Things get more interesting if you don’t give it a call syntax and just see what it does based on the name alone.

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text:
>  For example, when we served Kimi K2.6 with vLLM version 0.28, we got the expected tool call schema only 92% of the time. In other words, 2 out of every 25 attempted tool calls failed.
100% success is critical for tool calling.
The probability that the overall agent iteration is successful would scale very poorly even if we achieved 95%. With p95, if you need 50 tool calls that must execute sequentially to achieve a result, the chances that you
won't
have an error are only ~8%. There are ways to recover from bad tool calls (error feedback helps a lot), but if the agent is persistently using the wrong tools with the wrong args the overall system will not work very well.
